<reason>The motion is comparative ("more affordable"), and PRO owned that frame from the opening. The decisive thread: CON's arguendo that the counterfactual "trims prices a few percent" became the fulcrum. PRO's pressure question Q1 converted it into a concession of the motion, and CON's Rebuttal 2 walk-back ("ceiling, not an estimate") never rebuilt a positive case that the true effect is exactly zero — which, as PRO showed, requires an implausible horizontal demand curve contradicted by CON-admitted Houston/SF divergence. CON's Q2 demanded a mechanism for incumbent benefit, and PRO answered directly with the vacancy/renewal-letter channel and redirected bidding; PRO also turned Miami (glut/bust = supply moving prices down; narrow luxury strip; demand shocks; no counterfactual offered). CON's macro weighing (40% surge, doubled mortgage payments) was neutralized by PRO's correct point that it is baseline in both worlds and cannot decide a comparative motion. CON argued well — strong examples, the sprawl-adds-land vs infill-reprices-land distinction, memorable lines ("same world with cranes") — but each route was answered. Minor execution cost: PRO's Rebuttal 2 was clipped at the tail, though after its decisive point landed.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure question Q1 plus its repeated exploitation of CON's "trims prices a few percent" arguendo — it forced CON into defending literal zero price effect, an untenable burden, while PRO's A2 on Miami ("a glut is supply exceeding demand; a bust is prices falling") flipped CON's best example into evidence for the motion.</best_rebuttal>
